articles.text:
BAD LANDS COW BOY, BY A. T. PACKARD.

THE COW BOY is not published for fun, but for $2 per year.
Advertising Rates made known on application.
Standing Advertisements payable quarterly.
Transient Advertisements and all Job work, money in sight.
Address all communications to THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, MEDORA, DAKOTA.
articles.summary: Publisher's box: A. T. Packard's paper at $2 a year, with advertising and job-work terms.

articles.headline: INTRODUCTORY.
articles.text:
Unlike ninety-nine hundredths of the papers which have been started in the United States we do not come to fill a long-felt want. The cattle business here, though already of gigantic proportions, is still in its infancy in point of time. We do not come to [illegible] end. Another field would have been more congenial. We do not come as the agent or tool of any man or set of men. There is a wide field for us to cover, and we intend to cover it. We do come, however, to make some almighty dollars.

There is nothing like honesty, and now that we have come out thus plainly our motives cannot be impeached. But to fulfill our mission we must publish a good paper. We will not even be satisfied with this. Only when every one will acknowledge that ours is the best cattle paper in the Northwest will we be satisfied. Our beginning may be small, but [not?] nearly so much so as that of many another paper which now stands at the head. This, then, is next to our principal mission, to publish the best cattle paper in the Northwest and to preach King Cattle to all men. For the present, our inside pages will furnish sufficient general reading matter and our outside pages will be devoted almost exclusively to cattle and Bad Lands items.

In politics we are Republican clear through to the backbone, and will continue to be so as long as that party continues to merit the esteem of all fair-thinking men. Our allegiance to the Republican party is not such, however, as to blind us to its faults. In politics, as in all else, we will be free and out-spoken in our opinions. Whenever we see a wrong committed we will struggle with all our feeble might to have it righted.

To sum up, we intend to publish the best paper we can, sparing no expense in that direction, for we are confident that it will be "as bread cast upon the waters." It will return before many days in the shape of those same almighty dollars of which we have previously spoken.
articles.summary: Packard's opening editorial: the Cow Boy aims to be the best cattle paper in the Northwest, is Republican but independent, and frankly means to make money.

articles.headline: A WORD TO OUR SUBSCRIBERS.
articles.text:
To reach a paying basis, a newspaper must, of all things, be conducted on business principles. To secure the adoption of these principles, payments must be met as promptly as in every other business, that is every three months or sooner. With this in view we intend adopting a modification of the "cash in advance" system, namely, cash in hand or before the end of three months. Every subscription that is not paid up within that time will positively be taken from our list and what will be the subscriber's loss will be our everlasting gain.

All will understand that the editor is not out here for his health, as it is remarkably fine in any locality, and that the printers are not millionaires in disguise who tender their services gratis on account of their consuming love for the editor. We might also add, in this connection, that generous relatives have not contended with each other as to who should furnish us our outfit "without money and without price." Every thing from presses to galley rack was bought brand new from the best type foundry in the United States.

We suppose no one likes to be dunned. Every subscriber can save the ill-feeling a dun causes by coming to the office with the subscription price or handing it to us anywhere. If a subscriber should happen to be out of cash, furs of all kinds at the highest market price will be taken in payment. They are as good to us as the money, and deer hides will be bought in this way for twenty-five cents a pound, from five to seven cents more than can possibly be realized for them in cash.

If our subscribers will act upon these facts and thus avoid any seeming lack of confidence on our part by stopping the paper, it will greatly oblige the editor and enhance good feeling on both sides.
articles.summary: Subscription terms: payment within three months, with furs and deer hides (25 cents a pound) accepted in place of cash.

articles.text: We are glad to see that Mr. Howard Eaton has taken the initiative in the one thing that is now most important to our cattle men. We refer to the subject of cattle organization. In another column will be found the call for a meeting. This is a matter of vital interest to every stock man of the Bad Lands. Subjects continually come up that should be settled by the vote of the majority of our cattle men. At present there is no organization, and each man must decide all questions for himself. There is no need of recapitulating the list of benefits that will arise from this organization. They are patent to all. Every stock man must be in favor of it, and hence we look for a large meeting next Feb. 28. This date is an excellent one as it gives plenty of time to have matters which will come up for consideration at that time, considered beforehand and interferes in no way with the annual round-up. Every cattle man should and, probably will, arrange his business so as to be present. Each one should think of some matter that needs consideration, think it over carefully and be prepared with facts and figures upon it. This will avoid the loss of time and waste of wind that usually attends the beginning of an organization. Enough important matters will come up to occupy all the time that can be given to the meeting. This organization will be in the course of time, if not at once, one of the strongest in the Northwest. All then should attend the opening meeting which will be held at Little Missouri, the 28th of this month, at 10 A. M.
articles.summary: The paper backs Howard Eaton's call for a meeting of Bad Lands cattle men at Little Missouri on Feb. 28 to form a stockmen's organization.

articles.text: There is a feeling among a few of our cattle men that there are enough [illegible] here already, and that any attempt by new dealers to bring cattle to this point should be discouraged. We are happy to state that this feeling is not by any means universal. Every man who is here now has his range, which will not be interfered with in any way by new stock raisers. There is an abundance of unoccupied land and an increase in the number of cattle and cattle raisers will work to the advantage of all concerned. If the Bad Lands were full of cattle it would not decrease the price, as the demand is far in advance of the supply. Word comes from Kansas that the cattle sections there are overstocked and the cattle men there are looking to the Northwest for relief. To all these we would say, come. There is plenty of room and you will be made welcome.
articles.summary: The paper says the Bad Lands have room for more cattle and invites stockmen from overstocked Kansas.

articles.text: From the articles in some of our exchanges it would seem that about the only live topic their editors had was that of lying about Little Missouri. All sorts of stories are being published, the mildest ones implying that Little Missouri is a den of thieves and cutthroats. How this idea got about we are at a loss to understand. There has been but one attempted robbery here, and that one was perpetrated by a tramp, who was discovered in the act and ordered to leave town immediately, which he did. Far from being the hardest town, Little Missouri is as peaceful a one as can be found on the Northern Pacific. If our exchanges would have the manhood to publish articles in reference to Little Missouri which are made up from facts alone it will show that they have a regard for the truth which is more commendable than common among them.
articles.summary: Packard rebuts newspaper stories painting Little Missouri as a den of thieves, citing only one attempted robbery, by a tramp.

articles.headline: RATTLESNAKE ON TOAST.
articles.text:
A typical cowboy, fresh from his herd, went into a Cheyenne chop-house. The tables were all filled with the exception of one, at which the terror of the plains seated himself. As he pulled off his hat and untied the red bandanna handkerchief from around his throat, he looked disdainfully around. The nimble waiter brushed an imaginary bread-crumb from the cloth, whisked a bill of fare from the castor, and placed it before the festive and untamed youth.

"Take it away!" he snarled. "I can't eat that. I want rattlesnake on toast!"

"Rattlesnake on toast!" yelled the waiter.

"Rattlesnake on toast!" responded the cook.

There was a strange flutter among the guests at this strange order, and the cowboy was scanned by many curious eyes. He looked a little disconcerted at having his order so promptly taken, and glanced furtively toward the front of the house. He saw the cooks and waiters engaged in filling orders, and looking as solemn as graveyards after midnight. He assumed a nonchalent air and picked his teeth with his fork.

A cook deftly removed the skin from a pickerel, and cutting a strip the proper shape, placed it in a spider. The waiter who had taken the order came tripping back to the bold buccaneer of the pampas.

"Will you have your snake well done or rare?"

"Rare with milk gravy on it."

"Gimme that snake rare—milk gravy on the side," was hallooed to the cook.

"Snake rare; milk gravy—side," cook shouted back.

"Say!" said the bovine steerer as the waiter passed him, "I'll take it well done." "Make it well done." "Make it well done," was answered back.

The lariat wrestler began to grow nervous. The careless expression had left his eyes, and a soft, subdued, melancholy shade had taken its place. He fidgeted in his chair, and seemed to be nerving himself for an ordeal.

"Here you are, sir," said the culinary Ganymede, placing a dish in which was something nicely coiled, which looked like a fried specimen of the genus crotalus. "Have a little Worcester sauce? Gives a very fine flavor. Some folks like mushrooms with their snakes. Others prefer Chili colorow. A little salad dressing don't go bad. There's vinegar and olive oil in the castor. Will you have tea or coffee? Very fine snake. Caught yesterday. Fat and tender."

When the waiter was delivering himself of this eulogy on the meal the steer driver slowly shoved his chair back. His eyes bulged out and he became pale around the gills. "I don't think I'll eat anything. I ain't hungry," he said, as he rose unsteadily to his feet and reached for his hat.

"Maybe you'd prefer broiled moccasin," insinuatingly suggested the waiter. "No," he replied, as the ashen pallor deepened on his face, "I ain't a bit hungry." He cast another glance at the dish he had ordered, and made a break for the door. He forgot to "pay at the counter."
articles.summary: Humorous sketch (set in Cheyenne, not local news) about a cowboy who orders rattlesnake on toast and flees when it arrives.

articles.headline: ON THE RANGE.
articles.text:
Colorado sold 100,000 beef steers in 1883.

About 800,000 cattle were pastured in Nevada last year.

There are now over 9,000 head of cattle in the Smoky Hill Pool.

There have never been reports about the cattle as favorable as come from all sides this year.

Reports from all quarters indicate that there will be a rush of capitalists to the whole West to engage in the stock business.

The reports that many New Mexican cattle have died from want of water have been contradicted. An abundance of water is reported.

Near Kingmen, in Southern Kansas, many cattle have died from a new disease. There are symptoms of poisoning and there seems to be great pain near the heart. The affected cattle die in about two hours.

France is ahead of Great Britain in cattle and hogs, and behind in sheep, the figures being as follows: France has 11,750,000 cattle, 2,750,000 swine and 24,500,000 sheep. Great Britain has 2,902,000 cattle, 2,500,000 swine and 26,000,000 sheep.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

There is a prospect of a syndicate of St. Louis and Kansas gentlemen securing a lease of a large tract of grazing land in the Indian territory not far from Vinita. This is one of the finest grass sections anywhere to be found, and a lease will be a fortune to its owners.

South America is destined to be the next great beef-producing region of the world. It is estimated that in two years from now that the cattle in the Argentine Confederation will number 28,000,000, against 13,000,000 in 1877. The enormous increase in the number of cattle has brought down the price so that good fat steers are selling at $6 to $8.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

The Graphic says that a close guess as to the health of animals may be often made by feeling their pulse. In a horse, a good and strong but quiet pulse beats forty times a minute; in an ox, fifty to fifty-five; in sheep and pigs, not less than seventy nor more than eighty for ordinary health. It may be felt wherever a large artery crosses a bone. In a horse it is generally felt on the cord which crosses over the bone of the lower jaw in front of the curved position, or in the bony ridge above the eye, and in cattle over the middle of the first rib. In sheep it is, perhaps, easier to place the hand on the left side, where the beating of the heart may be felt. A rapid, hard and full pulse in stock points to inflammation and high fever; a rapid, small and weak pulse also to fever, but to fever accompanied by a poor and weak state of the subject. A very slow pulse in stock will often be found to indicate brain disease, while a jumping and irregular pulse shows something wrong with the heart.

The idea prevails in many parts of the country that the per cent of losses among range cattle in the Northwest during the winter season is very great—sufficiently so to render the business extra hazardous. The following statement may act as an eye-opener in the matter: Late in the fall of 1881, T. J. Allen drove [9,000?] head of Texas steers into the Niobrara river country about the line dividing Wyoming from Nebraska. Two thousand of them were turned on the range for the winter and gathered the next year. Out of the two thousand he found and took to market all but thirty-five head. Since that year he has found fourteen head of the missing ones, leaving but twenty-one lost out of two thousand, a shade over one per cent. Mr. Allen has had no men on the range since he gathered his stock in 1882, or he undoubtedly would have found some of the missing ones. There are other cases where equally as good showings can be made. This does not look like an "extra hazardous" business.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

There appears to be no question that in the far West prices of stock cattle are far in advance of corresponding prices for beef cattle. This condition of affairs would speedily bring about a crisis, if not a total collapse, in any other business than this, and bring ruin and embarrassment to those who have gone in at the recent range of prices. We do not believe it possible that this condition of affairs can or will be long maintained, because it is not natural, but do not anticipate that the settling of prices of range cattle will result in serious embarrassment to anybody. If the prices are too high, the growth of the younger animals will more than compensate for the difference, and the older ones, with their increase, at any price which may be called legitimate, will be worth another season far more than the animals without increase are rated this season. There is a possibility that a settling of prices will dissipate a moiety of anticipated profits, but it is a peculiarity of the live-stock business which has saved thousands from bankruptcy and brought success out of the most reckless management and unfavorable conditions, that no matter what price is paid, or what streaks of bad fortune are encountered, the stock will grow to the desired mark.—[Breeder's Gazette, Chicago.
articles.summary: Column of clipped range and cattle-trade notes from western and national stock journals (no Bad Lands items).

articles.headline: SPORTING NOTES.
articles.text:
For the gist of the majority of the following articles we are indebted to that prince of American sporting journals, The Mirror of American Sports.

Parole's earnings for the last eight years have been $82,184.[illegible]

The January turf meeting in New Orleans was almost a failure, owing to bad weather.

"Plunger" Walton still owes his racing debts in England. He has left a poor name behind him.

The largest amount won in purses by any driver last season was $[illegible]. J. A. Goldsmith was the driver.

The ball players who went South at the close of the season are now telegraphing back for advance money to pay their way home.

[illegible line] weight of the United States [illegible] Tom Gilmore for the championship of Canada.

The smallest pony in the world is the pet of Baroness Burdette-Coutts Bartlett. It is five years old and stands thirteen inches high.

The Sullivan party have been on a grand series of drunken sprees since the beginning of their tour, which was to "popularize the manly art."

Mr. Richard Dowse, of Chicago, on Jan. [illegible] skated 100 yards in eleven seconds, equaling the best record, which was made by Mr. Ennis, the champion for speed.

Malone, of Chicago, won the pool championship by a score of eight series of games won and none lost. He is without doubt the finest pool player the world has ever produced.

Pierre Lorillard has thirty-five horses in training for the coming season. [Remainder of column 7 heavily damaged in the scan; not transcribed.]

Andre Christol defeated Charles Bixamos in a Græco-Roman wrestling match at New Orleans, Jan. 10. Christol was the tutor in wrestling of Whistler and Muldoon, but will now have a hard struggle to down either. He taught better than he knew.
articles.summary: Clipped national sporting notes credited to the Mirror of American Sports; most of column 7 is too damaged to read.

articles.text: Send in your subscriptions to THE COW BOY.
articles.summary: Call for subscriptions.

articles.text: The Marquis de Mores is not expected back for a month or six weeks.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès is away and not expected back for a month or six weeks.

articles.text: Joe Pennell, Gill Kennedy and Tom Stack went down to Belfield Monday night.
articles.summary: Joe Pennell, Gill Kennedy and Tom Stack went to Belfield Monday night.

articles.text: Don't sponge THE COW BOY from your neighbor. Take it yourself and see how much better you will enjoy it.
articles.summary: Plea to subscribe rather than borrow the paper.

articles.text: The coal mine turns out a small quantity of coal every day. In the near future it will again be worked extensively.
articles.summary: The local coal mine is producing a little coal daily and will soon be worked heavily again.

articles.text: The mail is now taken on and left off at Medora. This makes it very convenient for our genial postmaster, Mr. Coughlan.
articles.summary: Mail is now put on and taken off trains at Medora, convenient for postmaster Coughlan.

articles.text: The pay-car came through Tuesday "which is why" the railroad boys all wear that don't-you-tread-on-the-tail-o'-me-coat air.
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific pay-car came through Tuesday.

articles.text: As soon as the backbone of winter is broken, the abattoir will be thoroughly cleaned and overhauled, preparatory to spring and summer work.
articles.summary: The abattoir will be cleaned and overhauled for spring and summer work once winter breaks.

articles.text: Even at this time there is not a carpenter here but that has all the work he can possibly do. There will be an excellent chance for a large number more in the spring.
articles.summary: Carpenters are fully employed and more will be needed in spring.

articles.text: We have received many visits from our friends and hope to receive many others. When in town give us a call whether we are acquainted or not. If we are not, it is time we were.
articles.summary: Invitation to call at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Messrs. T. Creighton and J. Kramer, of Chicago, and Geo. Pfenstiel, of Rockford, Ill., three of the Marquis' best butchers, left last week for a visit to their homes. They will return in a month, however, as their services can be ill dispensed with.
articles.summary: Three of the Marquis's butchers left last week to visit their homes in Illinois and will return in a month.

articles.text: Little Missouri and Medora are both destined to have a large and legitimate boom this year. The writer personally knows of three young and energetic business men who will start here, and many others are only waiting till spring opens.
articles.summary: The paper predicts a boom for Little Missouri and Medora, with three new businessmen coming.

articles.text: We wish to especially impress upon the minds of our Bad Lands subscribers that furs are as good to us as money. For subscriptions, advertising or job work we will take them in payment at the highest market price. Deer hides, for which eighteen cents is the highest price now paid, we will take at twenty-five cents a pound.
articles.summary: The paper takes furs and deer hides (at 25 cents a pound) in payment.

articles.text: The herd of cattle belonging to H. B. Wadzworth & Co., was the first herd put in below here. There are [1,800?] head in the herd, mostly yearling and two-year-old heifers. They were driven in last fall and up to the last report not a head had been lost from any cause. The Wadzworth brothers are so well satisfied with worth brothers are so well satisfied with their success that they will drive in as many more in the spring.
articles.summary: H. B. Wadzworth & Co.'s herd, the first put in below town, came through without loss and the brothers plan to drive in as many more in spring.

articles.text: Our subscribers and friends will confer a great favor on us if they will send us the names of any persons who may wish to subscribe to THE COW BOY. It is impossible for us to see every one, and a mere mention of the matter will induce many to subscribe. Let every subscriber appoint himself a committee of one to canvass among his friends. The general [result?] will be the name of almost every man in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Request for names of prospective subscribers.

articles.text: We intend starting a museum of Bad Lands curiosities, and our subscribers will greatly oblige us by bringing in anything they may find that is either curious or remarkable. Frank Moore has already given us a good start with one of the finest pieces of petrifactions it has ever been our lot to see. It is a petrified cedar knot which is almost transparent. Part of the knot has fallen out and the veins of the wood are perfectly plain. If our subscribers make a point of bringing in these articles we will soon have a collection of which to be proud.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy starts a museum of Bad Lands curiosities, beginning with a petrified cedar knot from Frank Moore.

articles.text: There have been few more marked successes in journalism than has been achieved by The Breeder's Gazette, of Chicago. Started about two years ago as a twenty-four page weekly paper, it has gone on steadily increasing in matter and interest, as well as in size, first to twenty-eight, then to thirty-two, and, finally, to thirty-six pages weekly. As a paper for such farmers as make live-stock breeding, in any of its departments, a leading feature of their business, we do not know where to find its equal. We can heartily recommend it to our patrons as the leading paper of its class in America. It is published in Chicago, by J. H. Sanders & Co.; price $3 a year. We can furnish it and our own paper together at $4 a year, cash, for both. Call at our office and examine it, or send to the publishers for a specimen copy.
articles.summary: Recommendation of the Breeder's Gazette, offered in a club with the Cow Boy at $4 a year.

articles.text: The new freight and mail route between here and Deadwood is all but an established fact. Pennell & Roberts and Marquis de Mores are the ones most prominently interested. The object of establishing the route is to give an outlet for all freight and mail between the Black Hills, intermediate points and the N. P. R. R. at Little Missouri crossing. Rates have already been made with the N. P. and C., R. I. & P. R. R's. Mr. Roberts is now on a tour of inspection to ascertain the most practicable route, and is expected back every day. In a few days the company will be in shape to contract for freight of all kinds and in any quantity. Teams are already here by which about [100,000?] pounds of freight can be transported. This is a large undertaking, but Messrs. Pennell & Roberts are two of the oldest freighters in the West, and they are determined to make a success of it.
articles.summary: A freight and mail route from Little Missouri to Deadwood and the Black Hills, backed by Pennell & Roberts and the Marquis de Morès, is nearly established; Roberts is scouting the route.

articles.text: The work-train was laid off here Monday. It will soon be running again.
articles.summary: The railroad work-train was laid off at Little Missouri on Monday.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper is on a business trip to St. Paul and Duluth. He is expected back next Monday.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper is away on business in St. Paul and Duluth, due back next Monday.

articles.text: Mr. A. M. Sinnot has been sick for some time with inflammatory rheumatism, but has now nearly recovered.
articles.summary: A. M. Sinnot has nearly recovered from inflammatory rheumatism.

articles.text: All who wish some of those fine pictures made at the tent gallery must call at once, as I shall stay but one week longer. C. E. FINN, Artist.
articles.summary: Photographer C. E. Finn's tent gallery will stay only one more week.

articles.text: Edwin Bulpin, who is now telegraph operator at Medora, has been appointed express, freight and ticket agent. His many friends will be pleased to learn of his advancement.
articles.summary: Medora telegraph operator Edwin Bulpin has been made express, freight and ticket agent.

articles.text: Mr. Z. [Hyde?] shot several beautiful snow birds yesterday and kindly left two at THE COW BOY office. They are entirely unknown East, and we have sent them to Ann Arbor, Mich., to be mounted for the museum there.
articles.summary: Z. Hyde shot snow birds and left two at the office, which were sent to Ann Arbor, Mich., to be mounted for the museum there.

articles.text: Mr. James Cook, Studebaker Bros.' adjusting agent, was here a day or two last week. We will back him against any man who travels for business ability and genial good-fellowship. May the sight of him gladden our eyes often.
articles.summary: James Cook, Studebaker Bros.' adjusting agent, visited last week.

articles.text: Several of Marquis' ponies were stolen from Matthew's camp a few days ago. Up to last accounts the thieves had not been overtaken, but they probably will be. This is the first horse-stealing case for a long time in the Bad Lands, and the thieves, if caught, should be so dealt with as to discourage any further pleasantry of this sort.
articles.summary: Several of the Marquis's ponies were stolen from Matthew's camp; the thieves had not been caught.

articles.text: James Beaumont and John Monroe are in from their ranches down the river. They have been unsuccessful with their sheep, losing a large number. The choice of breed in the first place was unfortunate. Good, hardy sheep of the long-wooled variety will do as well here as cattle. The small, short-wooled variety do not do well. Both kinds have been tried, and the one is as a great a success as the other is a failure.
articles.summary: Sheep ranchers James Beaumont and John Monroe, in from down the river, report losing many sheep of a short-wooled breed.

articles.text: Messrs. G. P. Byrd and Wm. Weeks, of Mandan, made a descent on Little Missouri and took the place by storm last Sunday. Our last sad farewell was taken of them as they were going toward Frank Moore's ranche. They were loaded down with a No. 12 shot-gun and seventeen pocket pistols. They have sent in twice for more ammunition for their pocket pistols, and hence we judge that they are doing immense execution.
articles.summary: G. P. Byrd and Wm. Weeks of Mandan arrived Sunday and went out to Frank Moore's ranch, heavily armed for a hunt.

articles.text: Geo. Fitzgerald met with a painful accident last week, which may cause him the loss of the third finger on his right hand. Coming down from Glendive he was showing his revolver to a person who wished to purchase one, and in breaking it to show the extractor, a cartridge exploded, the ball passing clear through the metacarpal bone of his right third finger. It is now doing very well and "Fitz" expects soon to have the use of his hand.
articles.summary: Geo. Fitzgerald shot himself through the right hand by accident while showing a revolver on the way down from Glendive.

articles.text: Last night was one of the most beautiful ever seen even in this country. It did not seem cold at all. No one wore overcoats, but everyone was comfortable. Even to our citizens it will doubtless be the greatest surprise to learn that the thermometer all the evening was not higher than [20?] degrees below. Not a breath of air was stirring, the moon shone beautifully from a perfectly clear sky and it was a positive pleasure to be out of doors.
articles.summary: A still, clear, moonlit night felt mild although the thermometer stood about 20 below zero.

articles.text: It is so customary to advertise every place where even a poor little jack-snipe bobs up his nose as a "hunter's paradise" that the words have lost their meaning. Hence we do not use that expression, but we do claim that beyond all doubt the Bad Lands furnish more game than any other place of equal area in the United States. From five hundred to five thousand pounds of venison saddles brought in at one time to Little Missouri is not an uncommon sight. The man who goes out for a day's shooting and only kills one deer is almost ashamed to tell of it. There are plenty of ponies here and experienced hunters to guide all hunting parties.
articles.summary: The paper claims the Bad Lands hold more game than anywhere in the country, with venison brought into Little Missouri by the thousands of pounds.

articles.text: Just as soon as the weather will possibly permit, ground will be broken for some of the many improvements that Medora will undergo this season. Among others the Marquis will build a brick block, containing two large store rooms on the ground floor, the floors above being used for offices, etc. A boarding house and restaurant are also on the list of improvements, besides a fine billiard hall. Numerous small residence houses will also be built, which will be a great convenience to many here and to the many more who are coming. Medora is destined to be a flourishing town and those who are about to seek homes in the West can do no better than to come here. The deeds for the sale of city lots will soon arrive and will be on exhibition, and lots will be sold at THE COW BOY office.
articles.summary: Planned Medora improvements: a brick block by the Marquis, a boarding house, restaurant, billiard hall and houses; city lots to be sold at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Upon reading one of our exchanges we were strongly reminded of the travesty of an ancient contraband to the effect that, "Folks as live in glass shacks hadn't best heave no dornicks." The paper referred to contained an article stating that several of the citizens in the town it represented had been "held up" after dark and the authorities were powerless to arrest the perpetrators. The preceding issue of the same paper contained an article on the lawlessness of Little Missouri, intimating that people were continually "held up" and that we were almost enduring a reign of terror. The moral obliquity of some newspaper men is only equalled by their cold, hard nerve in publishing such abominable lies made up out of whole cloth. There has never been a case of "holding up" in Little Missouri. There has never been a robbery here of any amount. A callow youth who did not seem to realize what he was doing, tried it one night, but was unsuccessful. He won't try it again in Little Missouri. We wish that exchanges would make a note of this matter, and, hereafter, if they wish to make their paper sensational, do it at the expense of some other town.
articles.summary: Packard denies an exchange's claim that Little Missouri suffers hold-ups, noting that paper's own town had them.

articles.headline: THE BAD LANDS.
articles.text:
THE BAD LANDS.

Their Worth to the Stock Man, Miner and Gardener.

Their Formation, Physical Characteristics and General Appearance.

There is a very general opinion in different parts of the country, that the Bad Lands are the most sterile and uninhabitable region on the face of the earth. The writer well remembers the impression of them he obtained in his very youthful days from the study of Guyot's geography. Almost the whole Northwest was covered with the mysterious words Mauvaise Terres. The teacher gave a very free translation to these words and added some explanatory remarks to the effect that they were totally unfit for the habitation of man or beast. Even birds flying across succumbed to exhaustion before reaching its limits, as no food of any kind was obtainable. It will create no surprise among many of our readers to be told that this opinion, but slightly modified, is still prevalent in many parts of the country.

In the first place, we wish to state that the French name Mauvaise Terres, was derived from the old Indian name for them, which signified a land bad to travel in. The French readily adopted this meaning and called them Mauvaise Terres. The present name is a literal translation of these words.

To the large farmer these lands are practically worthless. Only at rare intervals can a level piece of ground be found that is several hundred acres in extent. To the gardener, however, they are as valuable as any lands in the Northwest. The finest vegetables of all kinds grow in the greatest profusion. Small fruit does equally well, and doubtless large fruit would be a success, though it has not been tried up to the present.

To the stock raiser and coal miner, however, this is the king country of the world. In no other place are there to be found so many favorable conditions for the raising of stock. Bunch and buffalo grass cover almost every inch of the ground. The raw sides of buttes are the only places where splendid grazing cannot be found. On many of the buttes, however, the grass grows clear to the summit, the slopes being the favorite pasture lands of the cattle. Generally no hay need be cut as the grass cures standing, and keeps the cattle in as good condition all winter as if they were stall-fed. The only reason for putting up hay is to avoid a scarcity of feed in case of heavy snow. This very seldom happens, however, as very little snow falls in the Bad Lands. In spite of the numerous cuts of the railroad there never has been a blockade in the Bad Lands, although they are common over all the rest of the road. At no time this winter has snow been three inches deep on a level. A curious fact with cattle is that the ones that have been here a year or two and know how to rustle will turn away from a stack of hay, paw away the snow from the grass and feed on that, exclusively. Even in the dead of winter a meadow has a very perceptible tinge of green.

The Bad Lands are made up of buttes, ravines and coolies. The buttes are from one hundred to seven hundred feet high, some ending in a sharp peak, others having a table land at their summit containing from one to five hundred acres. The buttes are mostly in irregular ridges divided by ravines. At the [bottom?] of these ravines [invariably?] flows a stream of water, furnishing an abundant supply for cattle. These ravines are generally wooded, consisting of growths of cottonwood, cedar and ash. The ridges of buttes are cross-divided by small ravines called coolies. In the [bottom?] of these is a dense growth of small bushes, the [lurking?] place of thousands of deer, which come there to eat the tender twigs.

A stranger in the Bad Lands would generally be completely bewildered and lost before he had gone a mile. There is a continuous succession of coolies, ravines and buttes, which bear such a family resemblance to each other as to furnish no landmark whatever. To the initiated, however, there is no more danger of being lost than there is in his own native town. Every coolie slopes toward a ravine, every ravine either runs into the Little Missouri valley or else into some other ravine which does. Then remember that although the Little Missouri river is very crooked, the general direction while in the Bad Lands is directly north, and it is impossible to get lost.

The coal fields of the Bad Lands contain enough coal to supply the world. It is a superior quality of lignite and crops out directly on the face of raw buttes. We have yet to see one in which there were not from one to five veins of coal in plain view. In the course of time this will be a large source of income.

It is a hard task to describe the physical appearance of the Bad Lands. There is nothing in the world with which to compare them. They are unique. Perhaps a good illustration would be to take a bed of clay, harder in some places than others, wear it away in fissures by the action of water and then burn the whole into a solid mass, some of the peaks turning into brick. Enlarge this to proportions one hundred miles by thirty and you have a faint idea of the Bad Lands. Next to the feeling which the grandeur of the scenery provokes, perhaps the most lively motion experienced is that of the grotesque. The most fanciful creations everywhere [illegible]. Forts innumerable, bastions, siege guns, ruined castles, terraces, pyramids, cones and statues are a few of the most prominent caricatures. The whole might well be the work of an omnipotent Nast. Immense blocks of scoria on the summit of some of the buttes show vividly the effects of fire. Upon the very next butte not a sign of fire can be discovered. The slope of a butte may have a gentle, grassy ascent clear to its summit. Its neighbor's slope may be so rough, stony, steep and corrugated that even the mountain sheep shun its precipitous sides. There is no regularity whatever except the arragement of the large ravines and the level of the summits of the buttes. It is as though Pluto and Eolus had had a drawn battle lasting for centuries. These in turn gave place to the god of confusion and discord who now reigns supreme, above all and over all.
articles.summary: Long descriptive article on the Bad Lands: origin of the name, grazing, mild winters, coal, terrain and grotesque scenery.

articles.text: Medora would be a good place for a brick-kiln. Several brick buildings will be erected the coming summer and there is a large call for brick up and down the line. There is an abundance of clay everywhere and the masses of scoria testify as to its brick-making qualities.
articles.summary: The paper suggests a brick-kiln at Medora, with brick buildings coming in summer.

articles.headline: An Unpleasant Afterthought.
articles.text:
"Now," said drummer number one, as the train pulled out of Pittsburgh, "I have a bottle of whisky. Let's sit down and have a real good time. I only wish we had sugar and ice, we could have some to[ddy?]."

"I've got sugar," said drummer number two unstrapping his valise.

"And my brother has some ice," said drummer number three: "he's in the baggage car. I'll just step in and get some."

And he did.

The toddy was brewed and rebrewed. The whisky bottle was a large one, the supply of sugar seemed inexhaustible, and drummer number three made as many visits to the baggage car as the occasion demanded.

However, just as they were all feeling good and were about to compound a farewell drink, number three returned empty-handed.

"Very sorry boys," he remarked, "but the baggage man says if I take any more ice off my brother he won't keep."
articles.summary: Humorous filler (not local) about drummers taking ice from a corpse in a baggage car.
